content_html_sanitized:
Posted April 23, 2001
Special to MarijuanaNews by Richard Cowan

It has been my good fortune to have attended most of the NORML conferences, beginning with the first, in 1972. Over the years, these conferences have reflected the ups and downs of the marijuana reform movement. This year’s meeting was truly the most promising, although I have learned from hard experience that what happens after the conference is all that matters.

The keynote speech by retiring ACLU Executive Director, Ira Glasser, really was a " keynote " and set the tone for the conference.

I have heard Ira speak many times and he is always eloquent, but his " keynote " was a caution about balancing pragmatism and the need for important tactical victories with the need to keep our " eyes on the prize, " the ultimate objective of legalizing marijuana.

Happily, we are making enough progress, winning enough victories, so that is a realistic concern. For example, the passage of California’s Prop 36, which mandated treatment, rather than prison, for " drug possession " was a major defeat for the Drug Warriors, but coerced treatment is not really a victory for freedom. As it happens, Prop 36 does not apply to marijuana, which is decriminalized in California, but it is clear that the kinder, gentler drug war, prohibition with a human face, will inevitably try to force marijuana users into " treatment. "

Governor Gary Johnson’s speech at lunch on the first day was carried live on C-Span. This sort of coverage is invaluable.

It was also reported the next day in the Washington Post.

Typically, the Post put the story not in the hard news section but in the Style section, with a photo of Johnson, an All-American-boy type, that was chosen to make him look bad. The message was clear: " Don’t take this issue seriously. " Pravda was less slavish to the party line.

(The next day, they dutifully ran a column by DEA Director, Donnie Marshall, which they put on the Op-ed page. It was real gem. I talked about it on Saturday when I was on a panel on the Internet and Activism. I hope we can also put that on Pot-TV, and I hope to have more comments on it later, but in the meantime get a powerful anti-emetic and see )

Later on Thursday, San Francisco DA Terrence Hallinan, made a deeply moving speech. He had recently testified for the defense in the Sonoma Coounty medical marijuana grow operation case against Ken Hayes. He had the great pleasure of announcing that the jury had acquitted Hayes and his co-defendant after only a few hours of deliberation. This is a very significant victory for the medical marijuana movement, and Hallinan’s testimony certainly played a major role. Look for Hallinan to be even more aggressive in implementing Prop 215 in San Francisco. He is a genuinely fine human being. I hope to interview him soon on Pot-TV.

On Thursday, Eugene Oscapella of the Canadian Foundation for Drug Policy was unable to attend, so I filled in for him to give an overview of the situation in Canada. I hope that we can post that on Pot-TV later this week.

Thursday afternoon provided what was certainly the high point of conference in many ways. Dr. Lester Grinspoon offered a very personal and deeply moving account of his own marijuana use. He began by describing how he had deliberately delayed trying marijuana until after his book Marihuana Reconsidered had been published and he had testified several times on the subject. He also talked about how useful marijuana had been to him over the years as an aid to creativity and insight. Many of those who heard him told me that they were deeply moved by his candor and courage. His speech was a source of validation for many have who had similar experiences in their lives. Hearing so great a scholar talk about this was very reassuring.

One of the most interesting talks was given Friday by Bill Piper of the Lindesmith center. Piper had attended a ridiculous hearing held by the most rabid prohibitionists in the House of Representatives just before the March 28th Supreme Court hearing on medical marijuana.

What I found absolute fascinating was his account of the testimony of former California Attorney General Dan Lundgren. The prohibitionists on the committee, Barr, Souder, et al., had invited him, expecting to hear the party line. Amazingly, Lundgren, who remains an ardent prohibitionist, instead warned them that their sort of blind opposition to medical marijuana risked losing public support for the Drug War as a whole.

He is right, of course, but I doubt if any of these people are smart enough to understand this. The prohibitionists' greatest strategic problem remains the fact that the reefer madness crowd is their hard core constituency. For them, cannabis is simply an evil plant and the cannabinoids are wicked little molecules. Any compromise is heresy.

As I said in the beginning, what happens after the conference is all that really counts. What made me most hopeful for the future was the quality of the people who attended and the number of new faces. I made many new friends and I very much appreciate the kindness of the readers of MarijuanaNews and the viewers of Pot-TV.

The marijuana issue is clearly on the public agenda now and we are winning. The only question is how much damage will be done before the war ends.

One thing remains the same as in all the years before: There were far more people arrested everyday in DEAland on marijuana charges than attended the conference. That must change.
